One-page synthesis

Verdict: Read first. This is a high-value methods paper for researchers using OHDSI-style comparative cohort studies or deciding whether small sites should contribute to federated analyses. Its strongest contribution is not a universal sample-size cutoff, but a demonstration that conventional maximum standardized-difference diagnostics can falsely reject small datasets while bias reduction may remain useful.
Core thesisLocally fitted, high-dimensional LSPS models often reduce systematic error even when site samples fall to 250–500 people, and local models usually perform similarly to a global model trained on the full 20,000-person sample.
Most actionable resultMaximum absolute standardized difference of means using a fixed 0.1 rule failed for every analysis at site sizes ≤4,000 in both databases, whereas a sample-size-aware significance diagnostic did not uniformly fail.
Bias–precision tradeoff1:1 matching generally produced lower EASE than stratification, but stratification—especially with the global model—often retained greater precision after empirical calibration.
Main cautionSome target–comparator pairs retained substantial residual bias, particularly at smaller site sizes; statistical power was often poor, with Type II error frequently above 0.25–0.50 even at larger sizes.

What the evidence supports

SOURCE-DERIVEDAcross most of six drug comparisons in two databases, propensity-score adjustment reduced EASE relative to unadjusted analyses. Matching was usually more resilient than stratification for bias reduction, and local models were often close to global-model performance.

What the evidence does not support

APPRAISALThe results should not be converted into a rule that “n = 250 is safe.” Performance varied by target–comparator pair and database, and the simulated sites lacked real cross-site differences in coding, prescribing, geography, and population composition.

Study question and design

ElementStudy implementation
QuestionHow reliably do locally fitted LSPS models balance covariates and reduce treatment-effect bias when individual distributed-network sites have small samples?
Population/dataNew users of selected antihypertensive, antihyperglycemic, and antidepressant drugs, with ≥365 days of prior observation and indication-specific diagnoses.
Methods comparedLocal LSPS models, one global LSPS model applied within sites, and unadjusted analyses; each PS model used either 1:1 matching or 10-stratum stratification.
ControlsReal negative-control outcomes from LEGEND studies and synthetic positive controls with true hazard ratios of 1.5, 2, and 4.
Site-size experimentA 20,000-person sample was partitioned once into 5×4,000, 10×2,000, 20×1,000, 40×500, or 80×250-person non-overlapping sites.
Primary evaluation conceptsExpected Absolute Systematic Error (EASE), calibrated precision, Type I error, Type II error, maximum standardized difference, and a sample-size-aware SMD significance test.
Scale6 clinical comparisons × 2 databases × 156 fitted populations/subsets = 1,872 propensity models.

Section condensation

Abstract

SOURCE-DERIVEDThe study addresses whether high-dimensional LSPS models remain useful when individual observational-data sites are small. It partitions two large real-world databases into simulated sites, fits local LSPS models, and evaluates balance, bias, calibrated precision, and error rates using negative and synthetic positive controls.

SOURCE-DERIVEDThe authors report generally reliable bias reduction, greater small-sample resilience for matching than stratification, misleading failure of standard balance diagnostics, and improved performance from a chance-adjusted significance diagnostic. They conclude small sites should not be discarded solely because conventional standardized-difference rules fail.

Introduction

SOURCE-DERIVEDThe rationale is that federated networks often contain sites too small to support conventional confidence in propensity-score modeling. LSPS differs from manually specified PS models by using L1-regularized regression over thousands of generic covariates, supporting scalable and reproducible adjustment within OMOP/OHDSI studies.

SOURCE-DERIVEDThe paper separates covariate balance from treatment-effect bias. It argues that fixed standardized-difference thresholds can flag chance imbalance when thousands of covariates are examined in small samples, and that bias should be assessed across many sites and control outcomes rather than inferred from balance alone.

Methods — data, cohorts, and controls

SOURCE-DERIVEDCCAE claims and Optum EHR data were mapped to OMOP-CDM. Cohorts used a new-user comparative design, required 365 days of prior observation, excluded concurrent target/comparator membership, required hypertension, type 2 diabetes, or major depressive disorder as appropriate, and followed patients until a >30-day drug-supply gap.

SOURCE-DERIVEDCandidate comparisons were screened in CCAE using unadjusted negative-control estimates. EASE was modeled from a Gaussian distribution fitted to negative-control log hazard ratios, and the lower confidence bound of EASE guided selection. Negative controls assumed a true HR of 1; synthetic positives injected outcomes to create true HRs of 1.5, 2, and 4.

Methods — simulated distributed network

SOURCE-DERIVEDFor each comparison, the investigators sampled 20,000 eligible patients and partitioned that sample once at each site-size configuration. The local strategy trained one LSPS model in each site; the global strategy trained on all 20,000 and applied scores within each site; the unadjusted strategy omitted PS adjustment.

SOURCE-DERIVEDLSPS used L1-regularized logistic regression with the penalty selected by 10-fold cross-validated out-of-sample likelihood. Adjustment used 1:1 matching with a 0.2-logit caliper or ten equally sized strata. Person-level data were pooled after site-specific adjustment and analyzed with site-conditioned Cox models; the study deliberately did not evaluate summary-level meta-analysis performance.

Methods — metrics and diagnostics

SOURCE-DERIVEDPerformance metrics were EASE, geometric mean precision of calibrated log-HR estimates, Type I error among negative controls, Type II error among synthetic positives, maximum absolute standardized difference, and a significance test asking whether covariate differences significantly exceeded 0.1 after accounting for sample size.

APPRAISALThis metric set is unusually strong for a PS simulation because it does not equate balance with validity. Negative controls and calibration directly target residual systematic error, while the global model and unadjusted analysis provide practical upper and lower benchmarks.

Results — balance diagnostics

SOURCE-DERIVEDThe standard maximum absolute standardized-difference rule failed in both databases whenever site size was ≤4,000. The sample-size-aware significance test flagged fewer covariates, and meta-analyzing covariate balance across sites further reduced the number judged significantly imbalanced.

SOURCE-DERIVEDFailure was not eliminated for every comparison: some target–comparator pairs showed increasing numbers of significant imbalances as site size decreased. Matching consistently appeared better balanced than stratification in the significance-based diagnostic.

Results — systematic error

SOURCE-DERIVEDAdjustment reduced EASE in almost all settings. The principal exception was glimepiride–saxagliptin in CCAE, where unadjusted EASE was already low. Nortriptyline–fluoxetine in CCAE retained substantial residual bias, which worsened as sites became smaller.

SOURCE-DERIVEDThe global model sometimes reduced bias more than local models, but the pattern was not consistent. Matching generally yielded lower EASE than stratification and only rarely exceeded EASE 0.2.

Results — precision and error rates

SOURCE-DERIVEDAfter empirical calibration, PS adjustment generally improved precision, except for glimepiride–saxagliptin in CCAE and losartan–hydrochlorothiazide in Optum EHR. Stratification, particularly with a global model, produced the largest precision gains.

SOURCE-DERIVEDType I error was generally near 0.05 but varied for some comparisons, notably quinapril–propranolol. Power remained limited: Type II error often exceeded 0.25–0.50, including at larger sample sizes. Losartan–hydrochlorothiazide was the only comparison with consistently low Type I and Type II error across strategies in both databases.

Discussion and conclusions

SOURCE-DERIVEDThe authors interpret the local/global similarity as evidence that high-dimensional LSPS fitting may degrade less than expected at small sites. They favor matching when bias reduction is the priority and note that calibrated stratification may be preferred when precision matters and Type I error remains controlled.

SOURCE-DERIVEDThey recommend replacing sole reliance on fixed standardized-difference cutoffs with diagnostics that account for chance imbalance. Where residual bias remains high, they suggest adding prior confounder knowledge, dimensionality reduction, or cardinality matching, and call for validation in real independent federated databases.

Limitations, funding, and transparency

SOURCE-DERIVEDThe principal reported limitation is that sites were random partitions of national databases rather than independent healthcare systems. The experiment isolates sample size but omits real differences in population, coding, prescribing, and geography. Data cannot be publicly shared; aggregated data may be available on request, and analysis code is reported as public.

SOURCE-DERIVEDThe work was supported by an unconditional Johnson & Johnson methodological-research grant. Two authors were employees and shareholders of Johnson & Johnson; several authors or institutions reported related grants or contracts. These disclosures do not invalidate the results but are relevant when interpreting method selection and framing.

Figures and workflow

Evaluation and appraisal

Bottom line: The study provides credible, implementation-relevant evidence that small-site LSPS analyses can remain informative and that fixed SMD thresholds are unsafe as sole exclusion criteria. Confidence is moderate-to-high for the controlled simulation setting and moderate-to-low for real heterogeneous federated networks.

Main strengths

  • Uses two distinct real-world data modalities: claims and EHR.
  • Evaluates six clinically different target–comparator pairs rather than one synthetic scenario.
  • Uses real negative controls, synthetic positive controls, EASE, empirical calibration, and error rates rather than relying only on covariate balance.
  • Directly compares local models, an informative global benchmark, matching, stratification, and no adjustment.
  • Reports code availability and uses a reproducible OMOP/OHDSI stack.

Critical limitations

  • Simulated sites are random partitions of the same database and therefore lack true between-site heterogeneity.
  • Each 20,000-person sample is divided once at each configuration; repeated network-level partition replicates are not described.
  • Comparisons were selected using CCAE unadjusted bias, which enriches the evaluation for scenarios where adjustment can demonstrate improvement.
  • Person-level pooling avoids the small-count and heterogeneity problems of actual summary-level meta-analysis.
  • The study does not derive a validated site-level stopping rule, minimum sample size, or prospective decision algorithm.
  • Power is often limited, so apparently acceptable bias control does not guarantee useful detection of moderate effects.

9/10

Basis: Practical site-size and diagnostic decisions.

Limiting factor: Narrow focus on LSPS comparative cohorts.

Would rise: Prospective application in an active network.

Novelty
8/10

Rationale: Extends LSPS validation into small-site settings with direct bias and chance-adjusted balance assessment.

Basis: Combined controls, calibration, local/global design.

Limiting factor: Core PS methods are established.

Would rise: A validated operational decision rule.

Method strength
7/10

Rationale: Strong diagnostic framework and comparators, but the site simulation simplifies the federated problem.

Basis: 1,872 models, two databases, six pairs, controls.

Limiting factor: Random partitions, one split configuration, person-level pooling.

Would rise: Repeated simulations and truly independent sites.

Evidence strength
7/10

Rationale: The data directly support the within-experiment claims and report uncertainty and error behavior.

Basis: EASE, credible intervals, Type I/II error, calibration.

Limiting factor: Evidence remains simulation-within-real-data rather than external validation.

Would rise: Replication in real federated networks.

External validity
5/10

Rationale: Two databases improve breadth, but random partitions do not reproduce cross-site heterogeneity.

Basis: Claims and EHR environments.

Limiting factor: No independent local databases or geographic systems.

Would rise: Multinational site-level replication.

Implementation value
8/10

Rationale: Clear implications for balance QA, PS-method selection, calibration, and inclusion of small sites.

Basis: OMOP-compatible code and explicit workflow.

Limiting factor: No turnkey accept/reject threshold.

Would rise: Pre-specified operational guidance validated prospectively.

Do not use this paper to claim: that LSPS is reliable for every n=250 site; that balance-significance testing proves absence of confounding; that local LSPS eliminates the need for calibration or negative controls; or that the results validate real federated meta-analysis.

Implementation and research takeaways

For study diagnosticsDo not automatically exclude a small site because one of thousands of covariates exceeds |SMD|=0.1. Add a sample-size-aware balance diagnostic and inspect residual bias using negative controls.
For method selectionPrefer matching when minimizing systematic error is the dominant goal. Consider stratification when calibrated precision is more important, provided Type I error and residual bias remain acceptable.
For federated protocolsPre-specify site-level PS fitting, balance significance testing, negative-control diagnostics, empirical calibration, and an escalation path for sites with persistent bias.
For softwareKeep local model fitting, adjustment, outcome estimation, calibration, and diagnostic reporting as separate reproducible stages. Record site size, retained patients, failed strata/matches, and model provenance.
For evidence synthesisDo not infer that person-level pooling results will transfer unchanged to summary-level meta-analysis. Evaluate small/zero event counts and between-site heterogeneity separately.
For future validationReplicate across independent databases, repeat random partitions, test additional treatment prevalence ratios and event rates, and derive prospective thresholds tied to bias and coverage—not balance alone.

Proposed operational reading of the paper

  1. Small sample size is a risk factor, not an automatic exclusion criterion.
  2. Conventional maximum-SMD rules are poorly calibrated for high-dimensional small samples.
  3. Balance is necessary but insufficient; negative controls and calibrated error behavior are more decision-relevant.
  4. Residual bias remains comparison- and database-specific, requiring explicit incomplete/failed results rather than forced estimates.
